items.title: Tesseract, cell first
items.note: Four nested squares: the w- and z-divisions compose.

items.title: Tesseract, turned 45°
items.note: The same solid on the diagonal — every edge still lands on a grid line.

items.title: Tesseract, far camera
items.note: w 9.0 / z 2.6. The nesting tightens as the camera pulls back.

items.title: Tesseract, near camera
items.note: w 4.2 / z 2.2. Strong perspective pushes the inner cell small.

items.title: Tesseract, turned and near
items.note: The diamond with the inner cells spaced wide apart.

items.title: Tesseract, flattened
items.note: w 14 / z 4: the four cells collapse towards two. The minimal reading.

items.title: 16-cell, axis first
items.note: The tesseract's dual. Four of its eight vertices project to the origin, so it reads as a cross inside a diamond. Wants a 5-module stroke: its arms converge on a point, and anything thinner dissolves into the halo.

items.title: 16-cell, turned 45°
items.note: The same solid as a square with an X — the boldest silhouette here.

items.title: 4-8 duoprism
items.note: A square ring times an octagonal one.

items.title: 8-8 duoprism
items.note: Two octagons multiplied. Octagon edges sit on 45s, so they survive the grid.

items.title: 8-8 duoprism, turned 22.5°
items.note: Half a step of rotation and the rings line up vertex to edge.

items.title: 24-cell
items.note: Self-dual, 96 edges — the densest subject that still reads. A rosette rather than a silhouette.

items.title: 3-cube in the w=0 plane
items.note: A plain cube for contrast: square in square, corners joined.

items.title: 3-cube, turned 45°
items.note: The same cube on the diagonal.

items.title: Tesseract, version 15
items.note: 77 modules instead of 65. More of the code is free, so the halo is finer grained — and every module is smaller for a camera to resolve.

items.title: 8-8 duoprism, heavy stroke
items.note: The same octagons at a 3-module stroke: solid rings, almost no interior.

items.title: Ink on paper
items.note: The safe one. Maximum contrast, every reader's best case.

items.title: Hyperspace red
items.note: #ff2b2b on white. Red is dark enough in the luminance channel to binarise.

items.title: Ink to red
items.note: A diagonal gradient. The light end is where a reader will struggle first.

items.title: Inverted
items.note: White on black, for the page's own background. Most modern readers invert happily; some older ones refuse outright.

items.title: Red dots
items.note: Circular modules drop the ink fill fraction, the hardest combination to read.

items.title: Rounded plate
items.note: A rounded white plate, for dropping on the black page as a sticker.
